Hyundai Finally Confirms Spring 2027 US Launch for the Ioniq 6 N Electric Performance Sedan
8 photos
Photo: Hyundai / edited
South Korea's largest automaker is bringing the Ioniq 6 N to America next spring. The electric performance sedan is listed by Hyundai Motor America with extremely limited availability for the 2027 model year.
Unveiled a year ago at AutoMobility LA, the Ioniq 6 N in North American spec was originally intended to hit showrooms during 2026. The company's latest model year info pushes the launch into spring 2027 without any explanation for the delay, though one has to consider that very few peeps will be willing to spend just around $60,000 for a compact-sized Hyundai sedan.
Pricing has yet to be confirmed, but we do know the Ioniq 5 N crossover retails from $59,900 before destination, taxes, and optional extras. Using this logic, the sleeker electric vehicle should cost more. Speaking of which, the Ioniq 5 N carries over unchanged for model year 2027.
Hyundai Motor America isn't bringing lesser versions of the Ioniq 6 to the United States for 2027, leaving the N as the only derivative. In a similar fashion to the 5, the 6 in N flavor uses a dual-motor setup that promises 166 kilowatts for the front drive unit and 282 kilowatts for the rear motor. That's 601 mechanical horsepower, with N Grin Boost mode unlocking a further 40 for up to 10 seconds at a time.
Maximum torque reaches 568 pound-feet (770 Newton-meters), and you need every bit of torque when you remember how heavy the Ioniq 6 N actually is. Despite packing an 84-kWh battery, the zero-emission sedan requires 3.2 seconds to hit 60 miles per hour (97 kilometers per hour).
Photo: Hyundai Its top speed is anything but interesting after Tesla cracked 200 miles per hour with the now-discontinued Model S Plaid. If you insist, Hyundai Motor America says that 159 miles per hour (256 kilometers per hour) is doable with the right tires. Thankfully, the South Korean automaker understands that performance means a lot more than merely straight-line performance.
The redesigned suspension geometry, electronically controlled dampers, performance rubber, and electronic limited-slip diff are some highlights, along with revised bushings, stronger axles, and various structural reinforcements for improved body control and steering response. Even the rear anti-roll bar is stronger. From a visual standpoint, the prominent rear wing helps the Ioniq 6 N stand out in the crowd.
A wilder-looking machine than its crossover-bodied brother, the newcomer rolls on forged wheels that wear Pirelli P Zero tires. The wheel-tire combo frames four- and single-piston calipers that squeeze on 15.7- and 14.2-inch discs, with regenerative braking capable of providing up to 0.6 Gs of deceleration in the most aggressive operating mode.
While it may feature a large battery and 800-volt goodies, the driving range is best described as abysmal for a 2027 model year electric vehicle. 245 miles (394 kilometers) is the most you can expect with a full charge, and that's awful by all accounts. Not only do you get more range from a base Chevy Equinox EV crossover, but even the Tesla Model 3 Performance offers more, specifically 316 miles (509 kilometers).
Another part certain customers may not like about the Ioniq 6 N is the N e-Shift thingy, which simulates a transmission through programmed torque adjustments and gear ratios. N Active Sound+ is a bit on the gimmicky side of electric performance driving as well, as is the ambient shift light system that uses the cabin's ambient lighting to indicate simulated shift points.
